readerAnswers.status: The document is a Statement of Interest—the government explaining its position to the court. It is not the court’s decision. What changed was the government’s intervention in the argument, not a new permission slip for everyone using AI.
readerAnswers.scope: The filing distinguishes the copyright questions at those stages. Its focus is copying works during training. The department argues that using articles to develop a tool that can generate responses has a different purpose from publishing those articles for people to read. It also argues that requiring developers to pay for permission to use works could make it harder for smaller AI developers to compete. These are reasons it gives the court for accepting its position.
readerAnswers.mechanism: The filing separates three things that can get bundled into “AI used someone’s work”. A developer first obtains material. During training, software adjusts numerical settings using examples, developing patterns it can apply later. The trained part that produces a response is the model. When someone uses it, the answer it produces is an output.
readerAnswers.dispute: The New York Times, one of the publishers involved, has accused OpenAI and Microsoft of copying its journalism without permission. Its 2025 annual report records its demand for compensation and a court order stopping conduct it alleges infringes its rights. Those are the company’s claims and requests, not findings that every disputed use is unlawful.
readerAnswers.legal-test: Fair use asks about the purpose of a use, the kind of work copied, how much was taken and its importance, and the effect on the work’s market or value. The factors are considered together, case by case. There is no magic number of words you can copy that automatically makes a use fair.
readerAnswers.action: Imagine AI gives you a paragraph very close to a newsletter you found online. This filing does not establish that you can put it in a client presentation. Ask the person responsible for the material, “What is our basis for using this passage?” A claim about the model’s training does not answer that question about your proposed use.
readerAnswers.next: When the next headline says the copyright fight is settled, look for who actually decided what. A court ruling addressing a particular use would be a different development from this government filing. This report covers the September 1 submission; we have not verified a later ruling on its argument. And the discussion is about US law, not automatic permission in every country.

terms.fair use: On September 1, the US Department of Justice submitted an argument supporting OpenAI in the New York copyright lawsuits. It urged the court to treat copying written work to teach AI patterns as fair use: certain uses US law permits without the copyright owner’s permission.

explainBack: DOJ submitted an argument about one use of copied works: training a model. Collecting material and distributing a later answer remain distinct uses, so this filing neither records a court ruling nor establishes a right to publish an output.
unseenTransfer: An organisation pays to license a training dataset and an employee later obtains an output nearly reproducing a third-party article. The existence of the training licence does not establish the employee’s rights to publish that output; the specific output use and relevant permission or other legal basis must be checked.
repairsMade: Changed litigation to lawsuits, expanded the department reference, and explained licensing payments as paying for permission before independent handoff.
limitations: Producer reasoning, not observed human comprehension or independent admission.
No later merits order verified; the article states this explicitly and covers the dated filing.
